subtopics.title: Event details and key highlights
subtopics.summary: The 17th National Panchayati Raj Day was observed on 24 April at Vigyan Bhawan, organised by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. The theme was Sashakt Panchayat, Sarvangeen Vikas. The day marks the enforcement of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment and highlights initiatives such as the National Panchayat Awards and the Panchayat Advancement Index 2.0.
facts: The 17th National Panchayati Raj Day was observed on 24 April.
The event was held at Vigyan Bhawan.
It was organised by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
Theme: Sashakt Panchayat, Sarvangeen Vikas.
The day marks enforcement of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment, aimed at grassroots democracy and decentralised governance.
National Panchayat Awards recognise best-performing panchayats.
Panchayat Advancement Index 2.0 measures grassroots development and tracks panchayat performance.
e-GramSwaraj is used for transparent monitoring and data-driven governance.
Panchayat Dharohar Initiative is one of the key highlights.

subtopics.title: Committees on Panchayati Raj (1957-1986)
subtopics.summary: Several committees shaped the idea of Panchayati Raj before it was given constitutional form. The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended democratic decentralisation, and Rajasthan became the first state to establish Panchayati Raj, at Nagaur, on 2 October 1959. Later committees under Ashok Mehta, G.V.K. Rao and L.M. Singhvi reviewed the system: the Ashok Mehta committee recommended a two-tier system, the G.V.K. Rao committee reviewed administrative arrangements for rural development and poverty alleviation programmes, and the Singhvi committee recommended constitutional recognition of panchayats.
facts: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) examined the Community Development Programme (1952) and the National Extension Service (1953).
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended democratic decentralisation, which came to be known as Panchayati Raj.
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj system.
Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959 was the first state to establish Panchayati Raj.
Andhra Pradesh followed Rajasthan in adopting the system in 1959.
The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977), appointed by the Janata Government, recommended a two-tier Panchayati Raj system.
The G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) reviewed administrative arrangements for Rural Development and Poverty Alleviation Programmes.
The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986), appointed by the Rajiv Gandhi Government, recommended that PRIs be constitutionally recognised, protected and preserved.
B.R. Mehta is known as the Father of Panchayati Raj and the Architect of Panchayati Raj.

subtopics.title: 73rd Constitutional Amendment: background and structure
subtopics.summary: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment bill was introduced in Lok Sabha in September 1991 by the Congress government under P V Narasimha Rao. It came into force on 24 April 1993 and added Part IX, The Panchayats, to the Constitution. The amendment also added an 11th Schedule and set a three-tier structure for panchayats in every State.
facts: The bill was introduced in Lok Sabha in September 1991 by the Congress government under P V Narasimha Rao.
The bill became the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
The Act came into force on 24 April 1993.
Madhya Pradesh was the first state to implement the 73rd CAA.
A new Part IX, titled The Panchayats, covers Articles 243 to 243-O.
An 11th Schedule was added, containing 29 subjects of panchayats (Article 243-G).
Article 243-B provides for a three-tier system: village, intermediate and district levels.
A State with population not exceeding 20 lakh may not constitute panchayats at the intermediate level.
The amendment aims at governance closer to people, inclusive development, localised planning, digital transformation and transparency.

subtopics.title: Elections, reservation, term and oversight
subtopics.summary: All members of panchayats at each level are elected directly, while chairpersons at the intermediate and district levels are chosen indirectly. The amendment provides for reservation of seats for SCs, STs and women, and sets a five-year term with time limits for fresh elections. A State Election Commission supervises electoral rolls and elections, and a Finance Commission reviews panchayat finances.
facts: Article 243-C: all members of panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels are elected directly.
Chairpersons at intermediate and district levels are elected indirectly, by and from amongst the elected members.
The village-level chairperson is elected in the manner the State Legislature determines.
Article 243-D: seats are reserved for SCs and STs in proportion to their population.
Not less than one-third of total seats, and of chairperson offices, are reserved for women.
Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes is not applicable to Arunachal Pradesh.
Article 243-E: a panchayat has a five-year term but can be dissolved earlier.
Fresh elections must be completed before expiry of five years, or within six months of dissolution.
Article 243-K: a State Election Commission supervises electoral rolls and the conduct of panchayat elections; its State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor.
Article 243-I: the Governor constitutes a Finance Commission every five years to review panchayat finances.

subtopics.title: Exemptions, Union Territories and PESA
subtopics.summary: Some states and areas are exempted from Part IX, including Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram. Article 243-L lets the President extend Part IX to Union Territories with exceptions, and it applies there except Delhi. The PESA Act, 1996, enacted under Article 243-M, does not apply to Sixth Schedule areas.
facts: Under Article 243-M, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram are exempted.
Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas in the 5th and 6th Schedule states are exempted.
Hill Areas of Manipur for which District Councils exist are exempted.
The Darjeeling district of West Bengal, where the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council exists, is exempted.
Article 243-L: the President may direct that Part IX applies to a Union Territory, with exceptions and modifications.
Part IX applies to all Union Territories except Delhi.
The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, known as the PESA Act, was enacted under Article 243-M.
The PESA Act, 1996 is not applicable to Sixth Schedule areas.
The 6th Schedule states are Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

quizzes.passage: National Panchayati Raj Day is an occasion to reflect on local self-government in India. The day marks the enforcement of a constitutional amendment that was aimed at strengthening grassroots democracy and decentralised governance. The bill for this amendment was introduced in the Lok Sabha in September 1991, when a Congress government was in office. The amendment is described as having several important effects. Inclusive development ensures the participation of marginalised groups in local decisions. Localised planning promotes need-based development in villages and districts. Digital transformation is also listed among its significant effects. The amendment added a new Part to the Constitution, titled The Panchayats, and a new schedule that lists subjects for panchayats. It provides for a three-tier structure of panchayats at the village, intermediate and district levels. The amendment also provides that a state with a population not exceeding twenty lakh may skip the intermediate level of panchayats. It also provides for reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Madhya Pradesh was the first state to implement the amendment. The amendment's provisions are set out in Articles 243 to 243-O of the Constitution. Its provisions also deal with the term of panchayats, their finances and the conduct of their elections. Panchayats are the basic units through which these goals are pursued.

quizzes.passage: Panchayati Raj institutions are the system of local self-government that the amendment established in rural areas. The amendment added a new Part to the Constitution, titled The Panchayats, and its provisions are set out in Articles 243 to 243-O. Under this framework, panchayats function at three levels, namely the village, intermediate and district levels. The framework also provides for reservation of seats for women, so that women hold a set share of seats and offices in panchayats at each level. A panchayat can be dissolved before it completes its period, and when this happens fresh elections are needed to constitute a new panchayat. Such elections must be completed within a set period, and where the remaining period is short, an election need not be held. The amendment also added an 11th Schedule that lists subjects for panchayats. The bill for it was introduced in the Lok Sabha in September 1991 under a Congress government. The amendment's significance is described in three heads: inclusive development, which ensures the participation of marginalised groups; localised planning, which promotes need-based development; and digital transformation. Madhya Pradesh was the first state to implement the amendment. The framework was built to strengthen grassroots democracy and decentralised governance.

quizzes.passage: The Constitution's panchayat provisions do not apply uniformly to every part of India. Certain states and areas are exempted from the framework, and the amendment's rules set out these exemptions directly. These exemptions cover some states as well as some areas within other states. The framework was added as a new Part titled The Panchayats, consisting of provisions from Articles 243 to 243-O. Its provisions give panchayats a three-tier structure at the village, intermediate and district levels, and they provide for elections and for reservation of seats. The amendment also provides that a state with a population not exceeding twenty lakh may skip the intermediate level of panchayats. The amendment's significance is described under three heads: inclusive development, localised planning and digital transformation. The amendment also added an 11th Schedule that lists subjects for panchayats. Madhya Pradesh was the first state to implement it, and the bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in September 1991 under a Congress government. Its provisions also deal with the duration of panchayats and their finances. The provisions are meant to strengthen grassroots democracy and decentralised governance. Each of these features forms part of the framework described above.
